semantics.note: Keeps both parts: no utility on the scale of the cloud or smartphone booms, and very high costs. 'Enormous' fairly stands in for 'eye-watering'.

contract.note: The plain reading (widespread practical usefulness comparable to the early booms) is ordinary and fair. But the speaker gave no measure, comparison years or threshold, so the result depends on the evaluator's benchmark.

evidence.note: Spring 2024 survey: daily use is rare but some practical uses exist. There is no matched comparison with the cloud or smartphone booms, so it cannot settle the scale comparison.
2011 smartphone ownership is a different measure from routine generative AI use. Reference point only.
Estimated 2022 GPT-4 training compute cost. Earlier period, one company, training only.
Secondary report of projected OpenAI costs for 2024, not realised costs. One company only.

reviews.rationale: The utility comparison needs matched measures of adoption and benefit across generative AI and the early cloud and smartphone booms, and the packet has none. The cost evidence is estimates and projections for single companies, not realised industry-wide costs. Low routine use in e1 leans toward the claim but does not establish the comparison. Neither part is settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: 'At this point' becomes a present-state claim about publication time. That is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'effectively owns' as ownership-like practical control is the ordinary reading. The speaker's looser gloss about IP access is a separate sentence. A looser reading based on dependence alone could change the result.

evidence.note: The regulator's description of the 2023 agreements, which were in force in July 2024: OpenAI decides which models to build and what research to pursue. Weighs against ownership-like control. Some provisions are redacted.
Company disclosure of Azure exclusivity and compute dependence. Shows dependence, not control.
July 2024 Reuters: Microsoft's observer seat had no vote and was given up, and EU regulators said Microsoft does not control OpenAI. Microsoft's own description is an interested party's account.

reviews.rationale: On the contract's ownership-like-control reading, the evidence shows OpenAI kept decisions over research and models, Microsoft had no voting governance rights in July 2024, and EU regulators found no control. Azure dependence and IP access are shown, but the contract says those alone are not enough. Redacted terms leave some uncertainty.

contract.note: It uses OpenAI's own scale, as the speaker did. The criteria are clear and fair.

evidence.note: Contemporary report that OpenAI was on the cusp of level 2, so not yet past level 1.
Bloomberg, citing an OpenAI spokesperson: the company placed itself at level 1, and AGI systems did not yet exist.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from July 2024, attributed to an OpenAI spokesperson, says OpenAI placed itself at level 1 (chatbots), on the cusp of level 2, and that AGI did not yet exist. That matches the claim at publication.

contract.note: The contract correctly finds that 'true killer app' and the iPhone comparison have no determinate standard. It refuses to invent one, which is fair.

reviews.rationale: The central claim rests on an undefined evaluative standard: a 'true killer app' comparable to the iPhone. Adoption and capability data can inform the question but cannot decide it without adding a definition the speaker never gave. Not scored.
